claim: Monocytes, neutrophil cells, native B cells, plasma cells, T cells, and NK cells were identified from the CCLM samples.

claim: T and NK cells were the major components of all immune cells in CCLM samples.
source: Notably, T and NK cells were the major components of all immune cells and distinct across different tissue types, with NK cells significantly decreasing in tumor tissues (both primary colon cancer and liver metastasis cancer) compared to corresponding adjacent normal tissues, whereas T cells were the opposite (Figure 1D, E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text and references to Figure 1D, E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: NK cells significantly decreased in tumor tissues compared to corresponding adjacent normal tissues.

evidence: The claim is supported by the text and references to Figure 1D, E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: T cells increased in tumor tissues compared to corresponding adjacent normal tissues.

evidence: The claim is supported by the text and references to Figure 1D, E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Six morphological regions were identified in spatial transcriptomics: tumor, fibroblast, smooth muscle, B cells, hepatocytes, normal epithelium, and tumor and paratumor areas.
source: Furthermore, after combining the gene expression features of each sample (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, six morphological regions, including tumor, fibroblast, smooth muscle, B cells, hepatocytes, normal epithelium, and tumor and paratumor areas, were identified (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text and references to Figure 2A–C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: T cells were remarkably enriched in the tumor region of both primary colon cancer and liver metastasis cancer.
source: Consistent with scRNA-seq, T cells were remarkably enriched in the tumor region of both primary colon cancer and liver metastasis cancer, whereas NK cells were enriched in the non-tumor area (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text and reference to Figure 2D.

claim: NK cells were enriched in the non-tumor area of both primary colon cancer and liver metastasis cancer.
source: Consistent with scRNA-seq, T cells were remarkably enriched in the tumor region of both primary colon cancer and liver metastasis cancer, whereas NK cells were enriched in the non-tumor area (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text and reference to Figure 2D.

claim: The percentages of NK cells markedly decreased in metastasis colon cancer using MCPcounter, EPIC, and xCell.
source: The percentages of NK cells markedly decreased in metastasis colon cancer using MCPcounter, EPIC, and xCell (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text and reference to Figure 3A–D.

claim: A total of 1378 DEGs were determined between metastasis and non-metastasis colon cancer, including 817 upregulated and 561 downregulated genes.
source: A total of 1378 DEGs were determined using the limma package with cutoffs |log fold change| > 1.5 and p < 0.05, including 817 upregulated and 561 downregulated genes between metastasis and non-metastasis colon cancer.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text describing the data analysis.

claim: Cell killing, NK cell-mediated immunity, NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity, NK cell activation, and MHC-related GO terms were significantly enriched in DEGs between metastasis and non-metastasis colon cancer.
source: Subsequently, Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses were performed to investigate the correlative functions and pathways, As shown in Figure 3E, cell killing, NK cell-mediated immunity, NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity, NK cell activation, and MHC-related GO terms and the KEGG pathways of NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity were significantly enriched.
evidence: The claim is supported by the text and reference to Figure 3E.

claim: Nearly all the genes enriched in pathway of NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity were markedly downregulated in the metastasis group compared to the non-metastasis group.
source: Interestingly, nearly all the genes enriched in pathway of NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity were markedly downregulated in the metastasis group compared to the non-metastasis group (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text and reference to Figure 3F.

claim: NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity was enriched in the non-metastasis group.
source: Similarly, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that NK cell-mediated cytotoxicity was enriched in the non-metastasis group (Figure 3G, H).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text and reference to Figure 3G, H.

claim: Eight NK cell subtypes were identified through unsupervised clustering analysis.
source: Unsupervised clustering analysis of NK cells was thus performed and eight NK cell subtypes were thus identified (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text and reference to Figure 4A.

claim: NK cells were classified into three cell types: activated NK cells, resting NK cells, and other NK cells.
source: Combining the highly variable features of each NK cluster (Figure 4B) and CIBERSORT-reported canonical NK cell markers (Figure 4C, D), NK cells were classified into three cell types, including activated NK cells identified by the expression of KIR2DL4, GPR183, GRP171, CD69, and IFNG, resting NK cells marked by GZMK, TTC38, CD160, and PLEKNF1, and the other NK cells of which no characteristic gene was identified.
evidence: The claim is supported by the text and references to Figure 4B, C, D.

claim: Activated NK cells are identified by the expression of KIR2DL4, GPR183, GRP171, CD69, and IFNG.
source: Combining the highly variable features of each NK cluster (Figure 4B) and CIBERSORT-reported canonical NK cell markers (Figure 4C, D), NK cells were classified into three cell types, including activated NK cells identified by the expression of KIR2DL4, GPR183, GRP171, CD69, and IFNG, resting NK cells marked by GZMK, TTC38, CD160, and PLEKNF1, and the other NK cells of which no characteristic gene was identified.

claim: The expression of resting NK cells increased during disease progression.

Where serial samples were available from individual patients, the expression of resting NK cells increased, whereas that of activated NK cells decreased during disease progression (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text and references to Figure 4F, G.

claim: The expression of activated NK cells decreased during disease progression.
source: At the individual sample level, considerable variability was observed in the NK cell subset composition. Where serial samples were available from individual patients, the expression of resting NK cells increased, whereas that of activated NK cells decreased during disease progression (Figure 4F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by the text and references to Figure 4F, G.

claim: The gradient of the resting NK cells increased from adjacent normal colon tissues to primary colon tumor to liver metastasis tumor.

claim: The gradient of the activated NK cells decreased from adjacent normal colon tissues to primary colon tumor to liver metastasis tumor.

claim: The percentages of resting NK cells significantly increased in the metastasis group in the TCGA COAD cohort.

The percentages of resting NK cells significantly increased (Figure 5A), and the activated NK cells decreased in the metastasis group (Figure 5B), which is consistent with the scRNA-seq results.
evidence: The claim is supported by the text and reference to Figure 5A.

claim: The percentages of activated NK cells decreased in the metastasis group in the TCGA COAD cohort.
source: To evaluate the clinical relationship between NK cell differences and CCLM, CIBERSORT was performed using the TCGA COAD cohort. The percentages of resting NK cells significantly increased (Figure 5A), and the activated NK cells decreased in the metastasis group (Figure 5B), which is consistent with the scRNA-seq results.

claim: Resting NK cells were significantly increased in higher T, N, and TNM stages.

claim: Neutrophils and resting NK cells were associated with a worse prognosis.

claim: Activated NK cells and M1 macrophages were associated with better outcomes.

claim: Colon cancer patients with higher degrees of infiltration of resting NK cells had a significantly worse prognosis in the TCGA COAD and GSE29623 cohorts.

claim: Colon cancer patients with lower degrees of infiltration of activated NK cells had a significantly worse prognosis in the TCGA COAD and GSE29623 cohorts.

claim: Resting NK cells were remarkably enriched in the tumor region of both primary colon cancer and liver metastasis.

claim: KIR2DL4+ activated NK cells were lessened in proportion with the progression of the disease from normal colon to colon cancer and liver metastasis cancer.

claim: GZMK+ resting NK cells increased with the progression of the disease from normal colon to colon cancer and liver metastasis cancer.

claim: There was more infiltration of the KIR2DL4+ activated NK cell subset in the non-tumor area of both primary colon cancer and liver metastasis.

claim: GZMK+ resting NK cells were more infiltrated in the tumor region of both primary colon cancer and liver metastasis.

claim: Developmental routes were determined to begin with the KIR2DL4+ activated NK cells and then develop into GZMK+ resting NK cells.

claim: A mass of leukocyte differentiation and immune system process-related GO terms were significantly enriched in genes that change as NK cell subtypes move from the activated stage to the resting stage.

claim: NK cells slightly increased the expression of the resting marker GZMK upon exposure to tumor cells.

claim: The CD56brightCD16low NK cells that reside in secondary lymphoid tissues are immature and have reduced cytotoxic capability.

claim: Tumor-associated NK cells, which are enriched in tumors with impaired anti-tumor functions, were discovered to be associated with an unfavorable prognosis and resistance to immunotherapy in multiple solid tumors.
